scenes.title: NAT instances: operate the forwarding host deliberately
scenes.visual_overview: The left-hand packet path runs from private subnet instances through a NAT EC2 instance toward the internet; the right-hand panels emphasize the operational responsibilities and a managed alternative.
visual_walkthrough: Trace private subnet EC2 traffic into the NAT forwarding instance, then toward its public address and internet egress
Explain source/destination checking, forwarding software, subnet routes, source NAT, appropriate public subnet and return traffic
Review bandwidth, security, patching, scaling and failover responsibilities represented by the five icons
Compare managed NAT features without assuming those capabilities exist on a NAT instance
scenes.visual_example: A private subnet uses a self-managed NAT instance for outbound patch downloads; losing that host interrupts traffic unless a tested failover design exists.
scenes.visual_synthesis: NAT instance connectivity requires a functioning packet path and self-managed availability; prefer managed NAT when it better meets reliability and operations constraints.
scenes.narration: This slide covers a self-managed NAT instance, which is an EC2 machine forwarding outbound traffic for private subnets. Begin with the diagram on the left. Private subnet instances send their IPv4 traffic to the NAT instance through a deliberately configured route. The NAT host sits in a suitable public subnet, has internet connectivity through an Internet Gateway and a public IP or Elastic IP, and runs forwarding plus address translation software. The host normally needs source destination checking disabled because it forwards packets on behalf of other machines. Follow the return traffic as well: a route toward a NAT host is useless if the host stops forwarding or if return packets cannot traverse its state and the route back. Now move to the five operational icons at the top right. You own the EC2 instance bandwidth, security rules and hardening, patching, scaling and failover. A single NAT instance is itself a failure domain. The bottom-right panel shows why architects often evaluate managed NAT alternatives: they can reduce operations but have their own pricing, availability and routing design decisions. The exam distinction is simple: this legacy host can provide NAT when configured correctly, but it does not inherit automatic managed gateway resilience.

scenes.title: VPC Flow Logs: fields, NAT and observation points
scenes.visual_overview: Three side-by-side panels show how to read aggregate flow records, interpret recorded IP addresses near NAT and avoid overinterpreting ACCEPT or REJECT actions.
visual_walkthrough: Read ENI identifier, addresses, ports, protocol, packets, bytes, times, action and log status from the first panel
Follow original workloads through a NAT or inspection point and compare srcaddr/dstaddr with supported packet source and destination fields
Explain ACCEPT and REJECT as evidence at an observation point, not definitive root cause
Correlate both directions with route tables, security controls, application logs and collection scope
scenes.visual_example: A NAT-connected application appears to contact an unexpected IP in an ENI log; packet-level fields and the exact interface observation point may reveal address translation rather than malicious origin.
scenes.visual_synthesis: Use the field definition, interface and collection scope to interpret each flow; correlate with other evidence before diagnosing application or firewall behavior.
scenes.narration: The title asks us to understand what a VPC Flow Log can prove, not just to read ACCEPT or REJECT. Begin in the first panel. Each aggregated record describes traffic observed at a collection point, including its network interface, source and destination addresses and ports, protocol, packet and byte counts, time window, action and log status. It does not contain the application payload. The second panel introduces a NAT or middlebox between workloads and the wider network. At different interfaces, source and destination address fields can represent different observation contexts. Where supported, packet source and destination fields help distinguish original packet addresses from addresses seen after translation. The exact field definition and interface matter more than a familiar-looking IP. Finally move to the third panel: ACCEPT or REJECT is meaningful evidence, but it does not tell the entire cause of a failing application session. Traffic may be excluded, records can be delayed or skipped, and a security-group decision alone does not describe every routing or application failure. Correlate the outbound and return records with route tables, security policies, firewall and application logs. The key takeaway at the bottom is that interface, field semantics and collection scope define what your observation actually proves.
